messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 45
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Widowed
- Occupation: Military Medic
- Trauma Type: Natural disaster
- Pcl5: 66

He was a military medic, deployed with a forward surgical team to the coastal city that had been flattened by the earthquake. The runway was cracked, the air thick with dust and the smell of salt and rot. Within an hour of landing, he was standing in a makeshift triage tent, his gloved hands working on a young woman whose leg had been crushed by a concrete beam. He remember the sound—the wet, popping crack of bone as he tried to realign it, and then the scream that cut off when she went into shock. He worked for eighteen hours straight, pulling splinters of rebar from torsos, pressing gauze into wounds that wouldn’t stop bleeding, directing orderlies to stack the dead behind a row of overturned buses. At some point he realized the woman with the crushed leg had died while he was suturing someone else. He didn’t have time to close her eyes.

He returned home to his wife, alive, and he did not tell her about the leg or the stacks behind the buses. He told no one. He thought he was fine—medics are trained to compartmentalize, to move on, to treat the next casualty. But the next casualty did not come. Instead came the quiet of peacetime, the hum of the refrigerator, the sound of his wife’s breath beside him at night. He started waking up with his heart hammering, convinced the ground was shaking. He would lie still, listening for the rumble, his hand reaching for a tourniquet that wasn’t there. His wife asked him what was wrong. He said nothing.

Two years after the earthquake, she was diagnosed with ovarian cancer. He took a medical discharge to care for her. He became her full-time medic: scheduling appointments, mixing antiemetics, holding her hair back when she vomited. He was efficient, detached, always focusing on the next task. She wanted to talk about her fear, about the future. He told her there was no point in borrowing trouble. He was trained to treat the present wound, not the anticipatory grief.

She died on a Tuesday morning. He was holding her hand when her breathing slowed and stopped. He did not cry. He checked for a pulse, twice, then closed her eyes the way he had closed the eyes of strangers in the tent. He felt nothing except a kind of professional satisfaction that he had been there, that he had done his duty.

Now, three years after her death, he sits in my office. He says he came because his captain told him he was “too jumpy” on a training exercise last week—he threw a recruit to the ground when a helicopter passed low overhead. He speaks in a flat, clinical tone, describing his own behavior as if it belongs to someone else. He avoids the grocery store, he explains, because the fluorescent lights remind him of the triage tent. He no longer drives through the downtown area, where every leaning building feels like it’s about to fall. He hasn’t gone to his wife’s grave in eighteen months. He tells me that sometimes, in the middle of the night, he hears her voice saying his name, but he knows it’s just his own mind playing tricks. He has not dreamed of her. He dreams of the woman with the crushed leg—her face, her eyes, her one intact hand reaching up toward him. He wakes up and checks his hands for blood. He washes them anyway.

He says he is not suffering. He says suffering is for people who let themselves feel. He is a medic. He is trained to endure. His PCL-5 score is 66, and he tells me, without irony, that he wouldn’t know how to fill out an emotion questionnaire if it didn’t have a “none of the above” option. He folds his hands in his lap and waits for the next question, as if I am the trauma surgeon and he is the exposed wound that needs a quick, clean stitch.
